body.back: Derivatives. Decarboxylation gives biogenic amines: histamine, GABA, serotonin, dopamine, taurine.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Proteolysis. Hydrolysis of peptide bonds: digestive proteases (exogenous) and lysosomes, calpains, proteasome (endogenous).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Carbon skeletons. Glucogenic amino acids give glucose; leucine and lysine are purely ketogenic.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Transamination. Transfer of an amino group to an α-keto acid (pyridoxal phosphate); ALT and AST are liver markers.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Urea cycle. The liver converts toxic ammonia into urea excreted by the kidneys.

title: Define proteolysis and amino acid sources.
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: Define proteolysis and amino acid sources.
body.back: Hydrolysis of peptide bonds; amino acids come from dietary protein and recycling of body proteins.
Exogenous: pepsin, trypsin, chymotrypsin, carboxy-/aminopeptidases. Endogenous: lysosomes, calpain/calpastatin, proteasome.
Histidine → histamine; tryptophan → serotonin, melatonin; glutamate → GABA; DOPA → dopamine; cysteine → taurine.
Amino group transfer to an α-keto acid (PLP); ALT (alanine/pyruvate) and AST (aspartate/oxaloacetate) are liver markers.
Glutamate dehydrogenase releases NH₃; the liver's urea cycle converts it to urea excreted by the kidneys.
Glucogenic skeletons → glucose; ketogenic → acetyl-CoA, ketone bodies; Leu and Lys purely ketogenic.

Science integrating life with chemistry; structural, metabolic, clinical, analytical biochemistry.

title: General structure of an amino acid?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: General structure of an amino acid?
body.back: α-carbon bearing an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen and a side chain R.
22 proteinogenic (20 + 2); 9 essential: Phe, Val, Trp, Thr, Ile, Met, His, Leu, Lys; Arg conditionally essential.
α-carbon chiral (L/D); natural = L; glycine achiral.
At physiological pH amino acids carry −NH₃⁺ and −COO⁻: dipolar ion; amino acids are amphoteric.
Aliphatic, alcohol, sulphur, acidic, basic, amide, aromatic (UV-absorbing); polar vs non-polar.
Decarboxylation (His → histamine, Glu → GABA), amidation (Glu → Gln), oxidative deamination, transamination, PTMs.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Glycogen. Glycogenesis (insulin) and glycogenolysis (glucagon, adrenaline) in liver and muscle.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Glucose. Blood glucose 3.9-5.6 mmol/L (0.7-1.1 g/L); enters cells by GLUT or Na⁺-glucose symport.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Glycolysis. 10 reactions in 2 phases; regulation at hexokinase/glucokinase, PFK-1 and pyruvate kinase; net 2 ATP + 2 NADH.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Gluconeogenesis. Glucose from lactate, pyruvate, glycerol and glucogenic amino acids; bypasses 3 irreversible steps.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lactic fermentation. Without oxygen, pyruvate → lactate, recycled to glucose by the liver (Cori cycle).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pentose phosphate pathway. Cytosolic shunt producing NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate; key enzyme G6PD.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Aerobic oxidation. Pyruvate dehydrogenase, Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation: 30-32 ATP per glucose.
3.9-5.6 mmol/L (0.7-1.1 g/L); insulin lowers, glucagon and adrenaline raise.
Cytosol; 10 reactions (prep 1-5, payoff 6-10); regulated at hexokinase, PFK-1, pyruvate kinase; net 2 ATP + 2 NADH + 2 pyruvate.
Lactate (anaerobic; Cori cycle), ethanol (yeast), acetyl-CoA via PDH → Krebs → respiratory chain.
NADH 2.5, FADH₂ 1.5; total 30-32 ATP per glucose.
Malate-aspartate (liver, heart, kidney: 2.5 ATP/NADH); glycerol-3-phosphate (muscle, brain: 1.5).
UDP-glucose, glycogenin primer, glycogen synthase + branching enzyme; insulin; liver ~75 g, muscle ~250 g.
Phosphorylase, phosphoglucomutase, debranching enzyme, G6Pase (liver); glucagon, adrenaline; liver keeps blood glucose, muscle fuels contraction.
Liver and kidney; lactate, pyruvate, glycerol, glucogenic amino acids (not Leu, Lys); pyruvate carboxylase, PEPCK, FBPase-1, G6Pase.
Cytosolic; produces NADPH and ribose-5-P; key enzyme G6PD.

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Disaccharides. C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁: sucrose (Glc α1-2β Fru, non-reducing), lactose (Gal β1-4 Glc), maltose (Glc α1-4 Glc).

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Heteropolysaccharides. Glycosaminoglycans with two or more monomer types, bound to proteins as proteoglycans.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Homopolysaccharides. One type of monomer: glycogen (animal storage), starch (plant storage), cellulose (structural, β1-4).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Monosaccharides. CₙH₂ₙOₙ: glyceraldehyde and dihydroxyacetone (C3), ribose and deoxyribose (C5), glucose, galactose, fructose, mannose (C6).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Oligosaccharides. 2-10 units, e.g. on glycolipids and glycoproteins.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Polysaccharides. More than 10 units.
Hydrophilic polyhydroxylated molecules with one carbonyl group: aldehyde (aldose) or ketone (ketose).
Energy (primary fuel, glycaemia), structure (cartilage), nucleic acid components, metabolism.
By carbonyl (aldose/ketose) and carbon number: trioses, pentoses (ribose), hexoses (glucose, galactose, mannose, fructose).
D/L stereoisomers (D predominant); epimers (one carbon); α/β anomers after cyclisation.
Sucrose Glc α1-2β Fru (non-reducing); lactose Gal β1-4 Glc (reducing); maltose Glc α1-4 Glc (reducing).
Free anomeric OH or carbonyl; reduces Cu²⁺ to brick-red Cu₂O.
Glycogen (α1-4, α1-6 branches; liver, muscle), starch (amylose + amylopectin; plants), cellulose (β1-4; structural).
GAGs: heteropolysaccharides (hyaluronic acid, chondroitin sulphate); proteoglycans: GAGs on a protein core (mostly sugar); glycoproteins: mostly protein with short sugar chains.

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Oxidoreductases. Catalyse redox reactions, e.g. lactate dehydrogenase (NAD⁺/FAD).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Transferases. Transfer groups, e.g. glucokinase transfers phosphate.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hydrolases. Break bonds with water, e.g. proteases, pepsin, trypsin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lyases. Break or form bonds without water or oxidation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Isomerases. Rearrange a molecule into an isomer.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Ligases. Join two molecules using ATP energy.
Proteins (except ribozymes), catalysts lowering activation energy, recycled, low doses, no effect on yield or equilibrium, double specificity.
Common names end in -ase (except pepsin, trypsin); EC number: class, subclass, sub-subclass, enzyme.
Oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases.
Allosteric effectors (cooperativity), phosphorylation/dephosphorylation, association/dissociation of subunits.
Competitive (active site, overcome by substrate), non-competitive (other site), uncompetitive (enzyme-substrate complex only).
Mg²⁺ (kinases), Zn²⁺ (DNA polymerase, alcohol dehydrogenase), Fe²⁺ (catalase), Se (glutathione peroxidase).
TPP decarboxylation; FAD/FMN and NAD⁺/NADP⁺ redox; biotin carboxylation; CoA acyl carrier; PLP amino transfer; CoQ and cytochrome c electron transfer.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Acetyl-CoA. Enters the Krebs cycle; in the fasting liver it forms ketone bodies.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Activation. Fatty acid + CoA → acyl-CoA in the cytosol, costing the equivalent of 2 ATP.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: β-oxidation. Each turn removes 2 carbons as acetyl-CoA, producing 1 NADH and 1 FADH₂.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Transport. Carnitine carries long-chain acyl groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Palmitate yield. n = 8: 7 turns, 8 acetyl-CoA (80 ATP) + 7 NADH (17.5) + 7 FADH₂ (10.5) − 2 = 106 ATP.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lipolysis. Hydrolysis of triglycerides into glycerol and fatty acids.
IP3, DAG, phosphatidic acid (second messengers), free fatty acids (arachidonic acid → prostaglandins), membrane remodelling.
Activation to acyl-CoA (2 ATP), carnitine transport into mitochondria, β-oxidation (dehydrogenation, hydration, dehydrogenation, thiolysis).
C2n: n − 1 turns, n acetyl-CoA, n − 1 NADH, n − 1 FADH₂; palmitate ≈ 106 ATP.
Odd chains → propionyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA; unsaturated need extra isomerase/reductase steps.
Acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate, acetone; liver mitochondria; fasting, diabetes, high-protein diet; fuel brain, heart, muscle; excess → ketoacidosis.
Cytosol; malonyl-CoA; fatty acid synthase cycles (condensation, reduction, dehydration, reduction) to palmitate; elongases, desaturases; ω3/ω6 essential.
43 steps from acetyl-CoA, ATP and NADPH; HMG-CoA reductase (statins); derivatives: bile salts, vitamin D, steroid hormones.

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cholesterol. 80% synthesised, 20% dietary; membrane fluidity; precursor of steroid hormones, vitamin D and bile salts.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Fatty acids. Hydrocarbon chain + carboxylic acid; energy via β-oxidation; cis beneficial, trans (hydrogenated oils) harmful.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lipoproteins. Hydrophobic core with amphiphilic surface; five classes by density; high LDL → atherosclerosis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Prostaglandins. C20 mediators from unsaturated fatty acids; pain, inflammation, vasodilation; made by COX-1/COX-2, blocked by anti-inflammatories.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Phosphoglycerides. Glycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate + alcohol (choline, serine, inositol, ethanolamine): amphiphilic membrane lipids.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Sphingolipids. Membrane components such as galactocerebroside.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Glycerides. Esters of glycerol and fatty acids; triglycerides are strictly hydrophobic storage fat.
Organic molecules insoluble in water, soluble in organic solvents; strictly hydrophobic or amphiphilic.
Energy, membrane structure, metabolism, insulation (electrical: myelin; water; thermal and mechanical).
Hydrocarbon chain + COOH; saturated/unsaturated; cis vs trans; even carbons; β-oxidation.
Palmitic C16:0, stearic C18:0, palmitoleic C16:1 ω7, linoleic C18:2 ω6, α-linolenic C18:3 ω3.
Waxes, glycerides (TG), phosphoglycerides (lecithin), sphingolipids, sterols (cholesterol), prostaglandins.
Membrane fluidity; precursor of steroid hormones, vitamin D and bile salts; 80% synthesised.
C20 mediators from unsaturated fatty acids; pain, inflammation, vasodilation; COX-1/COX-2, inhibited by NSAIDs.
Hydrophobic core + amphiphilic surface; 5 classes by density; LDL (atherosclerosis), HDL; profile: TG, LDL-C, HDL-C, total cholesterol.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: DNA. Two antiparallel strands, hydrogen-bonded, in the nucleus and mitochondria; long and stable; about 3.2 billion base pairs.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Free nucleotides. Energy (ATP, GTP), second messenger (cAMP), coenzymes (NAD⁺, NADP⁺).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Nucleotide. Phosphate + pentose + nitrogenous base; a nucleoside lacks the phosphate.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: RNA. One short strand, in nucleus and cytoplasm; less stable; mRNA, rRNA, tRNA, microRNA.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Molecular biology. PCR amplifies DNA; next-generation sequencing reads it.
DNA stores genetic information; RNA expresses it; universal in all organisms.
Antiparallel double helix; phosphodiester bonds in strands, hydrogen bonds between A-T and G-C; ~3.2 billion bp.
Nucleotide: phosphate + pentose + base. Nucleoside: pentose + base.
Water-soluble, UV max 260 nm, heat denaturation (Tm, higher with GC), acid/base and nuclease hydrolysis.
Double vs single strand; deoxyribose vs ribose; T vs U; long and stable vs short and unstable; nucleus/mitochondria vs nucleus/cytoplasm.
mRNA, rRNA, tRNA, microRNA.
ATP, ADP, GTP (energy); cAMP (second messenger); NAD⁺/NADP⁺ (coenzymes).

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Denaturation. Heat (> 41 °C), extreme pH, solvents, salts, heavy metals, detergents or agitation unfold the protein; the primary structure remains.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Primary structure. The ordered sequence of amino acids, held by peptide bonds from N- to C-terminus.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Secondary structure. Local folding stabilised by hydrogen bonds: α-helix, parallel and antiparallel β-sheets, β-turns (proline, glycine).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Tertiary structure. Overall 3D shape from interactions between side chains; it determines function.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:biochem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Quaternary structure. Association of several polypeptide subunits.
Oligopeptide 2-10, polypeptide > 10, protein > 100 amino acids.
COOH + NH₂; strong, stable, planar, partial double bond, no rotation; N-terminal to C-terminal.
Glutathione (Glu-Cys-Gly, antioxidant); insulin (51 amino acids, β-cells, lowers glucose).
Primary: sequence. Secondary: α-helix, β-sheet, turns. Tertiary: 3D folding. Quaternary: subunits.
Fibrous: keratin, collagen, elastin. Globular: haemoglobin.
Glycoproteins (blood groups), lipoproteins (LDL/HDL), nucleoproteins (histones), phosphoproteins (casein), metalloproteins (haemoglobin, cytochromes).
Heat > 41 °C, pH 2-5 or ≥ 10, ethanol, high NaCl, redox agents, detergents, heavy metals (Ag⁺, Pb²⁺, Hg²⁺), agitation.
